assessment.nobel_worthiness: Very high. Nominal rigidities, staggered pricing and the New Keynesian framework are the working core of modern monetary policy analysis. Policy rules, forward guidance and inflation targeting rest on them, and central banks use them daily. The effect on both theory and practice is large and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread across many people. Calvo (time-dependent pricing) and Taylor (staggered contracts and the policy rule) supply foundational building blocks. Woodford provides the synthesis and the welfare-based normative framework. Gali, Gertler, Christiano and Eichenbaum, and Smets contributed to the estimated, medium-scale versions. The three-person limit means important contributors are left out.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature. The core ideas date from the late 1970s to the early 2000s, and decades of use, including through the 2008 and 2020s crises, have tested them.
uncertainties: The best three-person split of credit is genuinely contestable.
Post-2021 inflation and the limits of representative-agent versions may reduce the committee's appetite for this framework.
Overlap with earlier prizes on monetary policy and rational expectations (Lucas, Kydland-Prescott, Sargent-Sims, Bernanke) may be seen as a competing consideration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: High. The law-and-finance programme changed how economists understand the institutional determinants of financial development, ownership structure and investor protection. It opened a large empirical comparative-institutions literature, and its influence on research and policy debate is very broad.
assessment.attribution: The core LLSV papers are a clear collaborative unit, with Shleifer as the intellectual leader. Vishny is credited on the list, but his main joint work with Shleifer lies mostly in corporate finance and limited arbitrage rather than the legal-origins contribution itself.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with roughly 25 to 30 years since the 1997-1998 papers. The ideas have been widely tested and criticised.
uncertainties: Legal-origins causal claims have been seriously challenged on measurement and robustness grounds, and a committee might think the evidence is only partly settled.
Subsequent revisions by the authors themselves complicate the narrative.
Non-scientific controversies around some of the credited names could weigh on the decision, though they are not scientific evidence.
Overlap with the institutions prize in 2024 may affect timing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: High. Formal models of fairness and reciprocity, combined with experimental evidence, show that strategic behaviour and incentives depend systematically on non-selfish preferences. The work reshaped contract theory, public goods and labour-market analysis, and it generalises well beyond the lab.
assessment.attribution: Fehr is the central figure through the experimental evidence and the Fehr-Schmidt inequity-aversion model, and Schmidt is a natural co-recipient. Falk is credited for empirical and field extensions, but Bolton-Ockenfels, Rabin, Gächter and others made related contributions, and their omission is a real attribution concern.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The key papers date from 1999 to 2004, and replication and field evidence have accumulated over two decades.
uncertainties: Behavioural economics has already been recognised (Kahneman, Thaler), so the committee must judge whether this is a distinct contribution.
External validity of lab findings and of stable social preferences is debated.
The attribution boundary with Rabin, Bolton-Ockenfels and Gächter is blurry.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: High. Firm heterogeneity, selection into exporting and the resulting reallocation gains changed both theory and empirics of international trade. The framework has become the standard workhorse, linking micro data on firms to welfare analysis and policy.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the single most decisive contribution. Helpman has deep earlier credit in trade theory, and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work extends the framework to FDI versus exporting. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related contributions and are not credited here. Redding's contributions are valuable but later and less foundational.
assessment.maturity: Mature enough. Over two decades of use, extension and testing, with strong empirical confirmation of the basic facts about exporter heterogeneity.
uncertainties: Parallel contributions by Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum complicate the attribution.
Helpman's earlier trade work is also listed under B026, so the committee must decide which contribution to reward.
Trade was recognised by the 2008 prize (Krugman), and the committee may see this as an extension.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: High. The task-based approach to technology and the local labour-market evidence on import competition shaped the modern understanding of how technology and trade affect wages, employment and inequality. The policy and public debate impact is very large.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the central figure, through both the task framework with Levy and Murnane (the latter two not credited here) and the China-shock work. Hanson and Dorn are the natural co-authors of the China-shock design. Katz, who is also credited on this entry, has a distinct and foundational record on skill-biased technical change, so a different three-person split is plausible.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature. The task framework is more than 20 years old, and the China-shock results (2013 onward) have been replicated and refined.
uncertainties: Exposure-design identification, the persistence of effects and external validity have been questioned.
Overlap with the 2024 and 2025 laureates' work on technology and growth and with earlier prizes in labour economics.
The attribution of the task framework beyond the credited names is uncertain.
Capital-skill complementarity, which I know well, offers a competing structural view of the same facts, so I try to judge the empirical contribution on its own merits.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Moderately high to high. The misallocation framework gives a disciplined way to quantify how distortions in resource allocation across firms generate large cross-country productivity and income differences. It redirected the study of development and growth toward micro-level measurement.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) carry the headline measurement framework. Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) developed the closely parallel theory, and Rogerson is not on the credited list, which means that part of the credit may be misplaced. Restuccia is credited, but a pairing without Rogerson is awkward.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature, with about 15 to 17 years since the key papers. Measurement of misallocation is sensitive to assumptions, and the follow-up literature continues to refine the results.
uncertainties: Measured misallocation can partly reflect measurement error or unobserved heterogeneity in the data.
The two-person selection leaves out Restuccia and the unlisted Rogerson, an unavoidable attribution problem.
The magnitude of gains from removing distortions is debated, and the 2025 growth prize may reduce urgency.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: High and rising. Using population-scale administrative data, this work measured intergenerational mobility and its geographic variation, and it established a new empirical standard in public and labour economics. It has large methodological and policy reach, with strong credibility in design.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear leader of the programme. Hendren and Friedman are close co-authors on the key mobility and neighbourhood-effects papers. Katz, also credited, contributed to the Moving to Opportunity re-analysis and has an independent record, so a different split is possible. Chetty's other work (taxation, the elasticity of taxable income) may be treated as a separate line.
assessment.maturity: Less mature than the others. The central papers date from 2014 to 2022, and long-run follow-up and replication outside the US are still developing.
uncertainties: Recency makes it hard to tell whether the findings will hold up and prove foundational rather than data-driven.
Causal interpretation of neighbourhood effects and of place-based mobility rankings is contested.
Chetty also features in B037, and the committee may judge the overall oeuvre rather than one narrow discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: High on theoretical depth. The alternating-offers bargaining model gave a tractable strategic foundation for bargaining and a link to competitive outcomes in decentralised markets. It became a core building block in macro, labour (search and wage bargaining), political economy and market-design models.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (1982) is the decisive contribution. Rubinstein-Wolinsky (1985, 1990) extend it to markets. Binmore's role in the strategic bargaining literature and in earlier or related models is significant but secondary, and Stahl's earlier related work is not credited.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, more than 40 years old, with extensive use as a building block across fields.
uncertainties: Game theory has been recognised repeatedly (Nash-Harsanyi-Selten, Aumann-Schelling, Hurwicz-Maskin-Myerson, Milgrom-Wilson), so the committee may see saturation.
The model's main influence is as a modelling device, with fewer direct empirical or policy applications.
A narrow two-person split excludes Binmore, which could be contested.
